name: Thomson’s first absolute scale
summary: Thomson proposed a temperature scale defined by the work heat can do rather than by any substance, an early step towards absolute temperature.
description: A thermometric scale in which a unit of heat descending through any one degree yields the same mechanical effect, constructed from Carnot-style reasoning and an approximate use of Regnault’s steam data.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Carnot's theory suggested measuring temperature by mechanical effect, and Regnault's new steam data made an approximate calculation possible.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: October 1848 publication
date.basis: October 1848 Philosophical Magazine, volume 33, pp. 313–317, dates the published proposal.

events.statement: A thermometric scale in which a unit of heat descending through any one degree yields the same mechanical effect, constructed from Carnot-style reasoning and an approximate use of Regnault’s steam data.
events.caveats: This caloric-based 1848 proposal is not the later linear Kelvin scale. Thomson still expresses doubt about heat/work conversion and lacks reliable saturated-vapour densities across the full range.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 313–317, especially definition on p. 316 and data limits on p. 317
evidence.supports: Published scale definition, use of steam measurements, and limits of the calculation.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. community_entry.community: Scientific readers of the October 1848 Philosophical Magazine
community_entry.rationale: The published proposal exposed this particular 1848 scale to scientific readers.
community_entry.proxy_reason: No later independent use of this specific non-linear 1848 scale was established, so its dated publication is an awareness proxy, not acceptance.
community_entry.caveats: This caloric-based scale must not be conflated with the later linear Kelvin temperature scale; later adoption of this exact proposal is not established.

links.statement: Thomson stated that he knew Carnot’s theory through Clapeyron’s paper and used that theory in his 1848 thermometric-scale proposal.
links.scope: Thomson’s October 1848 paper, p. 313 footnote and pp. 315–316.
links.alternatives: Regnault’s measurements provided additional numerical input.
links.caveats: The source names Clapeyron’s 1834 paper and its English translation; it does not establish which physical copy Thomson used.
links.timing: 1834 original and 1837 translation precede the 1848 proposal.

evidence.supports: Explicit absence of access to Carnot’s original and named Clapeyron channel; scale argument.

links.statement: Thomson used Regnault’s measured latent heats and steam pressures to compare his proposed scale with the air thermometer, while identifying missing vapour-density data.
links.alternatives: Other thermometric substances and gas-law approximations were available; the historical calculation remained incomplete.
links.caveats: No claim that the calculated scale was fully verified across the entire interval.

evidence.supports: Explicit data use, approximate density assumptions and limits.
